title: 06 · Which test?
summary: Bradley's tests-of-inference tree: start with the kind of data, then what you compare; read p, and know the two ways to be wrong.
question: Which statistical test fits your data and your question, and how do you read its result?

chain.title: The decision tree
chain.statement: Choose a test in two moves: first the kind of data (measured, weakly measured, categorical counts, two variables), then what you compare.

explain.text: Measured data are continuous and roughly normal; weakly measured data are ranks, scores or non-normal; categorical counts say how many land in each group; two variables ask whether y is related to x. Each branch then splits by the comparison (one sample, two independent, paired, three or more), and every leaf names an R function.

figure.caption: Start with your data, then what you compare.

terms.meaning: a procedure that judges whether a pattern in a sample is likely to hold in the population

chain.intuition: The tree is a key, like the keys used to identify plants.
chain.misconception: Pick the test that gives a significant p. The data and the question choose the test before you see the result.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Choose by data and question, then run once.

check.q: Counts of flying and non-flying mammals in five danger levels: which branch?
check.a: Categorical counts: a contingency table, χ² test of association.

chain.opens: Which tests fit measured, roughly normal data?
chain.answers: Which statistical test fits your data and your question, and how do you read its result?

chain.title: Measured data: Z, t and ANOVA
chain.statement: For continuous, roughly normal data (check with hist() and shapiro.test(): p > 0.05 is normal enough): one sample with σ known → Z test; σ unknown → t.test(x, mu = 1.9); paired → t.test(a, b, paired = TRUE); two independent → t.test(y ~ group, data = dat); three or more → summary(aov(y ~ group)).

explain.text: All these tests compare means against the variation within the data. A Z test uses a known population σ: compute z, then the two-sided p is 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)). Usually σ is unknown and estimated from the sample, which widens the reference curve: that is the t distribution. Paired samples (the same subjects before and after) are tested on their differences; independent groups compare two means; with three or more groups ANOVA asks whether any mean differs.

figure.caption: The measured-data branch of the tree.

lines.explain: are the data close to normal? p > 0.05: normal enough
two-sided p for a Z test with z = 2.1
one-sample t test against the known mean 1.9

code.interpret: z = 2.1 is significant at the 5% level (p = 0.036).

examples.title: A paired t test on the classic sleep data (added)
examples.problem: Ten patients took two sleep drugs; extra hours of sleep were recorded for each drug (R's built-in data sleep). Does the second drug give more sleep?

solution.text: Each patient took both drugs, so the samples are paired: test the ten differences.
with(sleep, t.test(extra[group == 1], extra[group == 2], paired = TRUE)) gives a mean difference of −1.58 h, t = −4.06, df = 9.

examples.answer: p = 0.0028: the second drug gives about 1.6 h more sleep; very unlikely by chance.

source.title: The probable error of a mean

terms.meaning: two measurements on the same subjects; test the differences
analysis of variance: compares three or more group means at once
like the normal but with heavier tails, used when σ is estimated

chain.intuition: A t test asks whether the gap between means is large compared with the noise.

intuitionFigure.caption: t with 9 df; the sleep data's t = −4.06 lies far out in the tail.

chain.misconception: Paired data can be tested as two independent samples. That ignores that each subject is its own control and wastes power.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Before and after = one set of differences.

check.q: Weights of 12 rats before and after a diet: which call?
check.a: t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE) (if the differences are roughly normal).

chain.opens: What if the data are ranks or not normal?
chain.answers: Which tests fit measured, roughly normal data?

chain.title: Weakly measured data: rank tests
chain.statement: For ranks, scores or non-normal data: two independent samples → Mann–Whitney U, wilcox.test(y ~ group); two paired samples → Wilcoxon signed-rank, wilcox.test(a, b, paired = TRUE).

explain.text: Rank tests replace the values by their ranks (1st, 2nd, 3rd …) and compare the ranks, so a few extreme values or a skewed shape cannot dominate. They ask whether one group tends to have larger values than the other, rather than comparing means.

lines.explain: Mann–Whitney U: do two independent groups differ in their ranks?
Wilcoxon signed-rank: ranks of the paired differences

code.interpret: Use these when the histogram is skewed or the scale is only ordinal.

terms.meaning: the position of a value when all values are sorted
does not assume a specific distribution such as the normal

chain.intuition: A race result keeps the order and forgets the times.

wrong.title: Mistaken
wrong.text: One extreme value drags the mean.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Ranks: the extreme value is just "1st".

chain.misconception: Rank tests are always weaker, so avoid them. On skewed data they can be more powerful than a t test.

misconceptionFigure.caption: Fit the test to the data.

right.title: Instead
right.text: On skewed data they are often the better tool.

check.q: Pain scores 0–10 in two independent groups: which test?
check.a: Mann–Whitney U, wilcox.test(score ~ group): scores are ordinal.

chain.opens: Which tests fit counts in categories?
chain.answers: What if the data are ranks or not normal?

chain.title: Categorical counts: χ² and Fisher
chain.statement: Counts against an expected ratio → χ² goodness of fit, chisq.test(obs, p = props); two ways of grouping linked? → χ² test of association, chisq.test(table(a, b)); Fisher's exact test, fisher.test(table(a, b)), when an expected count is below 5. Use counts, never percentages.

explain.text: χ² adds up (observed − expected)² / expected over all cells: big gaps between what you saw and what the hypothesis predicts make a big χ². Percentages hide the sample size, and the test needs it, so always give the counts. With small expected counts the χ² approximation fails and Fisher's exact test is used.

figure.caption: Mendel's peas: observed counts against the 9:3:3:1 expectation (added example).

lines.explain: goodness of fit to the 9:3:3:1 ratio

code.interpret: The counts fit the 9:3:3:1 ratio very well: no evidence against it.

terms.meaning: total × the proportion the hypothesis predicts

chain.intuition: χ² measures the distance between the counts you saw and the counts you expected.
chain.misconception: chisq.test() works on percentages. It needs counts; percentages lose n and give wrong p-values.

check.q: A 2 × 2 table has a cell with expected count 3. Which test?

chain.opens: How do you test whether two variables are related?
chain.answers: Which tests fit counts in categories?

chain.title: Two variables: regression and correlation
chain.statement: Both well measured → regression lm(y ~ x) and correlation cor.test(x, y); ranks or weak measures → Spearman rank correlation, cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman").

explain.text: Regression fits a line and asks whether its slope differs from zero; correlation measures how tightly the points follow a line. For sheet 04's body mass and sleep, r = −0.53: cor.test() tells whether such an r could arise by chance with this n. Spearman does the same on ranks, for monotonic but not straight relations or ordinal data.

figure.caption: A line through two measured variables (shape of sheet 04's trend).

lines.explain: fit sleep as a straight-line function of log body mass
slope, intercept and the p-value of the slope
rank correlation for ordinal or non-linear data

code.interpret: The slope says how much sleep changes per tenfold increase in body mass.

chain.intuition: Regression draws the line; correlation says how tight the cloud is around it.
chain.misconception: A significant regression proves x causes y. In observational data it shows association only.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Significant slope → x and y go together.

check.q: Ranks of 8 wines by two judges: which test?

chain.opens: How do you read the p-value a test returns?
chain.answers: How do you test whether two variables are related?

chain.title: Reading p
chain.statement: p is the chance of a result at least this extreme if H₀ were true; p ≤ 0.05 → reject H₀ (≤ 0.01 highly, ≤ 0.001 very highly significant); p > 0.05 is no evidence of a difference, not proof of none.

explain.text: H₀, the null hypothesis, says there is no effect. A small p says the data would be surprising if H₀ were true. Testing many times inflates false alarms, so divide 0.05 by the number of tests (Bonferroni): with 5 tests, each must reach p ≤ 0.01.

figure.caption: The p scale of the sheet.

terms.meaning: null hypothesis: no effect or no difference
P(a result at least this extreme | H₀ true)
use 0.05 ÷ (number of tests) as the threshold

chain.intuition: p asks: if nothing were going on, how often would I see something this striking?

intuitionFigure.caption: Two-sided p for z = 2.1: both tails beyond ±2.1 (0.036).

chain.misconception: p is the probability that H₀ is true. It is the probability of data this extreme if H₀ is true.

misconceptionFigure.caption: Read p the right way round.

right.title: Instead
right.text: p = 0.03 → such data in 3% of samples if H₀ were true.

check.q: Ten tests: what threshold does Bonferroni give?

chain.opens: In which two ways can a test be wrong?
chain.answers: How do you read the p-value a test returns?

chain.title: Two ways to be wrong
chain.statement: Rejecting a true H₀ is a Type I error (a false positive, at rate α); not rejecting a false H₀ is a Type II error (a missed effect).

explain.text: α is the threshold you chose (0.05): when H₀ is true, you will still reject it in 5% of studies. A Type II error happens when the effect is real but the sample is too small or noisy to show it. If you predicted a direction before seeing the data, use alternative = "greater" (or "less"); otherwise test two-sided.

figure.caption: The four outcomes of a test.

lines.explain: one-sided: only a mean above 1.9 counts as evidence

code.interpret: Choose the direction before seeing the data.

terms.meaning: false positive: rejecting a true H₀
false negative: missing a real effect
the significance threshold, the Type I error rate

chain.intuition: A smoke alarm can ring without fire (Type I) or stay silent during one (Type II).
chain.misconception: Not significant means no effect. It may be a Type II error: the study may simply be too small.

right.title: Instead
right.text: p > 0.05 → no evidence; maybe too few data.

check.q: Lowering α from 0.05 to 0.01 makes which error rarer and which more likely?
check.a: Type I becomes rarer; Type II becomes more likely (real effects are harder to detect).

right.title: Instead
right.text: Smaller α: fewer false alarms, more missed effects.
